styles.name: Flat
styles.definition: A deliberately planar treatment that suppresses realistic surface modeling. Strict flat omits gloss and simulated relief; the related flat 2.0 vocabulary admits restrained depth cues. Neither names a substance.
styles.canonical_example: Windows 8 Metro and the flat examples in NN/g’s article; use the article’s flat 2.0 comparison to delimit the term.

styles.name: Material / paper
styles.definition: Google’s original Material uses paper as a model for layered surfaces, cast shadows and meaningful motion. Here “paper” means that opaque sheet-like recipe, not every generation or feature of Google Material Design.
styles.canonical_example: Material 1’s paper prototypes described by Christian Robertson; the documented layer/shadow experiments are the reference, rather than a guessed paper texture.

styles.name: Transparency
styles.definition: A compositing property: content behind a foreground contributes to the result according to alpha. It does not by itself imply blur, reflection, refraction or glass. Distinguish a partially transparent paint from opacity applied to an entire group.
styles.canonical_example: W3C’s source-over compositing diagrams, isolating foreground alpha from the backdrop.

styles.name: Glassmorphism
styles.definition: A frosted-glass aesthetic combining a see-through surface with a softened backdrop. Malewicz’s examples vary tint/gradient alpha, blur, edges and optional noise; the name does not designate one physical or platform implementation.
styles.canonical_example: The author’s four frosted card recipes and their border variations, including dark treatments.

styles.name: Acrylic (Fluent)
styles.definition: Microsoft’s translucent brush combines a backdrop, blur, an exclusion blend, tint and noise. Background acrylic samples behind the app; in-app acrylic samples within it. Microsoft supplies opaque fallbacks under conditions such as transparency being disabled.
styles.canonical_example: WinUI MenuFlyout, open ComboBox and AutoSuggestBox surfaces in Microsoft’s Acrylic guide.

styles.name: Mica
styles.definition: An opaque Windows foundation material influenced by the theme and desktop wallpaper, sampled once. It is not a live see-through pane. Mica Alt strengthens the wallpaper influence for uses such as tabbed title bars.
styles.canonical_example: Microsoft’s Mica window/title-bar and NavigationView examples; long-lived app foundations, including Settings.

styles.name: Liquid Glass (Apple, 2025)
styles.definition: Apple’s material joins lensing/refraction, responsive motion, highlights and adaptive separation. Regular adapts to content; Clear is more transparent and needs dimming for legibility. A blurred translucent card alone does not reproduce these behaviors.
styles.canonical_example: WWDC25’s toolbar-to-menu transition, floating sidebars and glass controls. Treat these as the native reference, not evidence of a complete CSS reproduction.

styles.name: Neumorphism
styles.definition: Objects appear extruded from, or pressed into, the same surface. Similar body/background colors plus opposed light and dark shading give soft relief; an independent floating card is a different cue.
styles.canonical_example: Alex Plyuto’s soft UI example reproduced in Malewicz’s article, and its illustrated inset pressed-state treatment. These are design demonstrations, not a platform component standard.

styles.name: Claymorphism
styles.definition: Inflated, rounded objects modeled with light and dark inner shading plus an external shadow. Unlike the same-surface neumorphic recipe, their color can stand apart from the ground.
styles.canonical_example: Malewicz’s inflated cards/buttons and construction sequence. The rounded, domed volume is characteristic; it is not a requirement to simulate granular sculpting clay.

styles.name: Skeuomorphism
styles.definition: A design retains recognizable ornamental features of a real-world predecessor to communicate what it is or does. It can use many materials; realism or a shadow alone does not establish that metaphor.
styles.canonical_example: The Kindle Fire wooden bookshelf shown by NN/g: shelves describe a real object used to organize books.

styles.name: Aqua
styles.definition: Apple’s original Mac OS X interface, announced in 2000, foregrounded luminous, semi-transparent controls and fluid interaction. Use the name for the historical language, not as a synonym for arbitrary glass.
styles.canonical_example: The launch announcement’s buttons, scrollbars, windows, Dock and Finder. Exact gloss geometry is not specified there.

styles.name: Frutiger Aero
styles.definition: CARI’s retrospective category joins glossy digital imagery, glass, natural imagery and humanist typography. It is an art-direction bundle rather than a single material or a synonym for Windows Aero.
styles.canonical_example: CARI’s curated archive and linked Asadal Design Mall case study; Microsoft’s archived Aero icon examples provide a vendor-authored example of the reflective icon vocabulary.

styles.name: Glow / neon
styles.definition: A luminous mark is given surrounding bloom so it reads as a light source. This is a style assembled from a core mark and glow effects; the surrounding surface need not itself be emissive.
styles.canonical_example: Erica Larson’s Adobe tutorial wraps a magenta neon triangle around a wrist using outer and inner glow plus masking.

styles.name: Gradient fill — linear
styles.definition: Color stops vary along a straight gradient axis. The result can shade a surface, but its colors and direction need not describe lighting.
styles.canonical_example: CSS Images 3’s linear-gradient figures and stop-placement examples.

styles.name: Gradient fill — radial
styles.definition: Color varies outward through circles or ellipses from a center. A radial fill can suggest a highlight or halo without being either physically.
styles.canonical_example: CSS Images 3’s circular/elliptical radial-gradient figures.

styles.name: Gradient fill — conic
styles.definition: Color varies by angle around a center. This angular field differs from the outward progression of a radial gradient.
styles.canonical_example: CSS Images 4’s color-wheel and conic-gradient examples.

styles.name: Gradient fill — mesh
styles.definition: A network of mesh points and patches distributes color in multiple directions. A mesh is not just another stop list on one axis; similar-looking freeform gradients should identify their actual construction.
styles.canonical_example: Adobe Illustrator’s multicolored ellipse and its editable mesh diagram.

styles.name: Gradient stroke
styles.definition: A gradient paints an outline instead of the interior. It can imply a lit edge, but that interpretation is optional.
styles.canonical_example: Photoshop’s documented Stroke effect with Gradient as its fill type.

styles.name: Inner shadow
styles.definition: An inset shadow is clipped within the subject; a dark edge commonly suggests a cavity. The geometry and interpretation are separate.
styles.canonical_example: CSS Backgrounds’ inset box-shadow examples.

styles.name: Inner glow
styles.definition: Glow is drawn inside the subject boundary. Its name describes location, not proof that the object emits light.
styles.canonical_example: Photoshop’s Inner Glow layer effect.

styles.name: Outer glow
styles.definition: A softened luminous halo extends outside the subject. This can decorate a mark without establishing cast-shadow depth.
styles.canonical_example: The outer-glow stage of Adobe’s neon triangle tutorial.

styles.name: Drop shadow
styles.definition: An external shadow projects the subject’s silhouette. Offset, spread and softness shape it; a zero-blur expanded silhouette can instead serve as a ring.
styles.canonical_example: CSS Backgrounds’ outer box-shadow diagrams.

styles.name: Bevel / emboss
styles.definition: Highlights and shadows model an edge or relief. Bevel describes the edge profile; emboss gives a raised impression, with inverted/debossed treatments suggesting a recess.
styles.canonical_example: Photoshop’s Bevel & Emboss effect and its style/light controls.

styles.name: Letterpress
styles.definition: A screen simulation of an impression pressed into a surface. Dark interior shading with a displaced lighter edge can make text read as debossed; ordinary offset text shadow alone is not sufficient evidence of that intent.
styles.canonical_example: José Olarte’s Fireworks-to-CSS worked text demonstrations. This is simulated impression, not a claim about every physical letterpress printing process.

styles.name: Grain
styles.definition: Fine spatial variation applied as texture. Photoshop’s Grain exposes amount, size and roughness; procedural noise is another construction, not evidence that all grain shares one distribution.
styles.canonical_example: Photoshop’s Grain adjustment workflow; W3C feTurbulence illustrations show a procedural alternative.
